problem: Footnote f is essentially the 1862 wording ("curious details concerning the introduction ... the first Act which prohibited the importation of them"); only the race term was changed.
replacement: f [ See Beverley’s “History of Virginia.” See also, in Jefferson’s “Memoirs,” some interesting details about how Black people were first brought into Virginia, and about the first Act, passed in 1778, that prohibited their importation.]

problem: Force softened: source says these consequences "suffice to explain many of the differences"; candidate has "go a long way toward explaining".
replacement: The State of Kentucky was founded in 1775, the State of Ohio only twelve years later; but twelve years count for more in America than half a century in Europe, and today the population of Ohio exceeds that of Kentucky by two hundred and fifty thousand souls. *j These opposite consequences of slavery and freedom are easy to understand, and they are enough to explain many of the differences we see between the civilization of antiquity and that of our own time.

problem: Nuance shifted: "This cultivation is specially carried on by slaves" (especially) became "Slaves do most of that work", a different claim (a majority).
replacement: l [ One particular reason helps turn the last two States away from the cause of slavery. This part of the Union used to draw its wealth mainly from growing tobacco. That crop is grown especially by slaves; but in the last few years the market price of tobacco has dropped, while the value of slaves has stayed the same. So the ratio between the cost of production and the value of the produce has shifted. The people of Maryland and Virginia are therefore more willing than they were thirty years ago to give up slave labor in tobacco growing, or to give up slavery and tobacco together.]

problem: Awkward English: "it matters to send him off" does not carry "it is important to export" naturally.
replacement: A State feels the lack of free hands more as its slaves become fewer. But the more the work is done by free hands, the less productive slave labor becomes; the slave is then a useless or burdensome possession, and it is important to send him off to those Southern States where the same competition is not to be feared. Thus the abolition of slavery does not set the slave free: it merely transfers him from one master to another, and from the North to the South.
